paras: The peonage case of Frank Hatten was a federal prosecution in Alabama in August 1915, in which Rhett Flemming, a Coffee County farmer, was charged with holding Hatten, a Black laborer, in peonage. On August 18 Flemming was bound over to the federal grand jury at Dothan after Hatten testified that he had been brought back to work each time he left and had once been whipped for about two hours with a leather strap.

Hatten worked for Flemming, whom the Montgomery Advertiser described as "a well known farmer of Coffee County." The report does not say how Hatten came to work for Flemming, how long he stayed, or where in the county the farm lay.

According to the report, Hatten left Flemming on several occasions but "is said to have been brought back and put to work." Hatten testified that on one occasion Flemming whipped him for about two hours with a leather strap. Neither the whipping nor the returns to work are dated in the coverage, and the report does not name anyone besides Flemming as taking part.

Hatten brought the complaint as plaintiff, and Flemming was arraigned on August 18, 1915, before Federal Commissioner C. S. Tutwiler at Dothan. Tutwiler bound Flemming over to await the action of the federal grand jury under $500 bond. No report of an indictment or trial was found in the coverage through the end of September 1915.

The case appears in a single short item, a special dispatch from Dothan printed by the Montgomery Advertiser on August 19 under the headline "COFFEE COUNTY FARMER IS HELD FOR PEONAGE." The item ran on page 7 beneath a card of thanks and reported the charge and Hatten's testimony without comment, calling him "the plaintiff" and "the negro" and hedging the forced returns with "is said to have been." No coverage of the case was found in other white papers or in the Black press.
